Psalms 1.summary: The blessed man does not walk with the ungodly but delights in the law of the LORD and meditates on it day and night (Psalm 1:1–2). He is "like a tree planted by the rivers of water" (Psalm 1:3). The ungodly are like chaff the wind drives away, and they will not stand in the judgment (Psalm 1:4–5). "For the LORD knoweth the way of the righteous: but the way of the ungodly shall perish" (Psalm 1:6).
Psalms 1.whereWeAre: Job ended with Job restored after meeting God. Psalms opens Israel's book of songs and prayers, and Psalm 1 sets out two ways: the blessed man who delights in the law of the LORD, and the ungodly who blow away like chaff. Psalm 2 turns to the nations and God's king.

Psalms 2.summary: The nations rage and their kings plot "against the LORD, and against his anointed" (Psalm 2:1–3). God laughs at them and says, "Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion" (Psalm 2:4–6). The king tells of the LORD's decree, "Thou art my Son," and of the nations given to him (Psalm 2:7–9). The kings are warned to serve the LORD with fear and "Kiss the Son" (Psalm 2:10–12).
Psalms 2.whereWeAre: Psalm 1 showed the blessed man and the ungodly man. Psalm 2 shows the nations raging against the LORD and his anointed, while God sets his king on Zion. Psalm 3 begins David's prayers in trouble.

Psalms 3.summary: Fleeing from Absalom, David says many rise against him and claim God will not help him (Psalm 3:1–2). "But thou, O LORD, art a shield for me," he says, and he lies down and sleeps because the LORD sustains him (Psalm 3:3–6). He asks God to save him, for "Salvation belongeth unto the LORD" (Psalm 3:7–8).
Psalms 3.whereWeAre: Psalm 2 ended, "Blessed are all they that put their trust in him" (Psalm 2:12). In Psalm 3 David puts that trust to the test as he flees from his son Absalom. Psalm 4 is an evening prayer.

Psalms 4.summary: David asks the God of his righteousness to hear him (Psalm 4:1). He asks how long men will love vanity and tells them, "Stand in awe, and sin not" (Psalm 4:2–5). God has put more gladness in his heart than a rich harvest brings (Psalm 4:6–7). He ends, "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep" (Psalm 4:8).
Psalms 4.whereWeAre: Psalm 3 was David's prayer in danger, sleeping safely among enemies. Psalm 4 is an evening prayer that ends, "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep" (Psalm 4:8). Psalm 5 is a prayer for the morning.

Psalms 5.summary: David says, "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD" (Psalm 5:1–3). God takes no pleasure in wickedness, but David will come into his house in fear (Psalm 5:4–7). He asks God to lead him past enemies whose "throat is an open sepulchre" (Psalm 5:8–10). Those who trust in God will rejoice, for he blesses the righteous like a shield (Psalm 5:11–12).
Psalms 5.whereWeAre: Psalm 4 ended with sleeping in peace. In Psalm 5 David prays in the morning for God to lead him and protect him from liars. Psalm 6 is a cry for mercy in sickness and grief.

Psalms 6.summary: David asks the LORD not to rebuke him in anger but to have mercy, for his bones are vexed (Psalm 6:1–3). He asks God to save him, saying, "all the night make I my bed to swim" with tears (Psalm 6:4–7). Then he tells the workers of iniquity to depart, for "the LORD hath heard the voice of my weeping" (Psalm 6:8–10).
Psalms 6.whereWeAre: Psalm 5 asked God to guide David past his enemies. In Psalm 6 he weeps all night for mercy, then knows the LORD has heard him. Psalm 7 asks God to judge him fairly against a false accuser.

Psalms 7.summary: David asks God to save him from those who would tear him like a lion (Psalm 7:1–2). He says that if he has done wrong, let the enemy take him (Psalm 7:3–5). He asks the LORD to rise and judge him by his righteousness (Psalm 7:6–11). The wicked man falls into the pit he dug, and David praises the LORD most high (Psalm 7:12–17).
Psalms 7.whereWeAre: Psalm 6 ended with God hearing David's weeping. In Psalm 7 David asks God, the righteous judge, to defend him against Cush the Benjamite. Psalm 8 turns to praise for God's glory in creation.

Psalms 8.summary: David begins, "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" (Psalm 8:1–2). Looking at the moon and stars, he asks, "What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" (Psalm 8:3–4). God has made man a little lower than the angels and given him dominion over the animals (Psalm 8:5–8). The psalm ends as it began, praising God's excellent name (Psalm 8:9).
Psalms 8.whereWeAre: Psalm 7 ended with praise to "the name of the LORD most high" (Psalm 7:17). Psalm 8 praises that name in all the earth and wonders why God cares for man. Psalm 9 thanks God for judging the nations.

Psalms 9.summary: David praises the LORD with his whole heart for turning back his enemies (Psalm 9:1–6). The LORD judges the world in righteousness and is "a refuge for the oppressed" (Psalm 9:7–10). David calls Zion to sing, for God does not forget the cry of the humble (Psalm 9:11–14). The nations fall into their own pit, "For the needy shall not alway be forgotten" (Psalm 9:15–20).
Psalms 9.whereWeAre: Psalm 8 praised God as Creator. Psalm 9 praises him as judge, "a refuge for the oppressed" (Psalm 9:9). Psalm 10 continues it, asking why God seems far away.

Psalms 10.summary: The psalmist asks, "Why standest thou afar off, O LORD?" (Psalm 10:1). The proud wicked man hunts the poor, curses, and says in his heart, "God hath forgotten" (Psalm 10:2–11). The psalmist asks God to arise and remember the humble, for God sees mischief (Psalm 10:12–15). "The LORD is King for ever and ever," and he hears the humble and defends the fatherless (Psalm 10:16–18).
Psalms 10.whereWeAre: Psalm 9 praised God for defending the poor. Psalm 10 asks, "Why standest thou afar off, O LORD?" (Psalm 10:1), and describes the wicked who prey on the helpless. Psalm 11 answers with trust.

Psalms 11.summary: When friends tell David, "Flee as a bird to your mountain," he answers that he trusts in the LORD (Psalm 11:1–3). "The LORD is in his holy temple," and his eyes test the righteous and the wicked (Psalm 11:4–5). He will rain fire on the wicked, for "the righteous LORD loveth righteousness" (Psalm 11:6–7).
Psalms 11.whereWeAre: Psalm 10 ended with the LORD as King for ever. In Psalm 11 friends tell David to flee, but he answers that the LORD is in his holy temple. Psalm 12 laments a world full of lies.

Psalms 12.summary: David cries, "Help, LORD; for the godly man ceaseth," and everyone speaks with flattering lips (Psalm 12:1–4). The LORD says he will arise for the poor and needy (Psalm 12:5). "The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times" (Psalm 12:6–8).
Psalms 12.whereWeAre: Psalm 11 ended with God seeing the upright. Psalm 12 complains that the godly are gone and everyone lies, but "The words of the LORD are pure words" (Psalm 12:6). Psalm 13 asks how long God will wait.

Psalms 13.summary: David asks, "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" (Psalm 13:1–2). He asks God to answer before he sleeps the sleep of death (Psalm 13:3–4). "But I have trusted in thy mercy," he says, and he will sing to the LORD (Psalm 13:5–6).
Psalms 13.whereWeAre: Psalm 12 lamented a land full of flatterers. In Psalm 13 David asks four times, "How long?" and then chooses to trust God's mercy. Psalm 14 describes the fool who says there is no God.

Psalms 14.summary: David writes, "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Psalm 14:1). The LORD looks down from heaven and finds that "there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Psalm 14:2–3). The workers of iniquity eat up God's people, but God is with the righteous (Psalm 14:4–6). David longs for the salvation of Israel to come out of Zion (Psalm 14:7).
Psalms 14.whereWeAre: Psalm 13 ended in song. Psalm 14 says, "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Psalm 14:1), and longs for salvation to come out of Zion. Psalm 15 asks who may live with God.

Psalms 15.summary: David asks, "LORD, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill?" (Psalm 15:1). The answer is the one who walks uprightly, speaks the truth in his heart, and does not slander his neighbor (Psalm 15:2–3). He keeps his promises even when it hurts and takes no bribe, and he "shall never be moved" (Psalm 15:4–5).
Psalms 15.whereWeAre: Psalm 14 described a world that has gone astray. Psalm 15 asks who may dwell in God's holy hill and answers with a picture of an honest life. Psalm 16 delights in God as David's portion.

Psalms 16.summary: David asks God to preserve him and delights in God's people (Psalm 16:1–4). "The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance," he says, and "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places" (Psalm 16:5–6). Because the LORD is at his right hand, he will not be moved, and God will not let his Holy One see corruption (Psalm 16:7–10). "In thy presence is fulness of joy" (Psalm 16:11).
Psalms 16.whereWeAre: Psalm 15 described who may live near God. In Psalm 16 David says the LORD is his portion and that God will not let his Holy One see corruption. Psalm 17 asks God to hear a just cause.

Psalms 17.summary: David asks the LORD to hear his just cause, for God has tested his heart (Psalm 17:1–5). He asks God, "Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings" (Psalm 17:6–9). His enemies are like a lion greedy for prey, and he asks God to rise and rescue him (Psalm 17:10–14). He will be satisfied when he wakes and sees God's likeness (Psalm 17:15).
Psalms 17.whereWeAre: Psalm 16 ended with "fulness of joy" in God's presence (Psalm 16:11). In Psalm 17 David asks God to keep him "as the apple of the eye" (Psalm 17:8) from his enemies. Psalm 18 celebrates his rescue.

Psalms 18.summary: David says, "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer" (Psalm 18:1–3). In his distress he called on God, and God came down in storm and fire to rescue him (Psalm 18:4–19). God rewarded him for keeping his ways, for "As for God, his way is perfect" (Psalm 18:20–30). God trained his hands for war and gave him victory over his enemies (Psalm 18:31–45). "The LORD liveth; and blessed be my rock," David says, for God shows mercy to David and his seed for evermore (Psalm 18:46–50).
Psalms 18.whereWeAre: Psalm 17 asked God to rescue David. Psalm 18 is his song of thanks on the day God delivered him from Saul and all his enemies. Psalm 19 praises God in the heavens and in his law.

Psalms 19.summary: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psalm 19:1–3). The sun runs its course like a bridegroom, and nothing is hid from its heat (Psalm 19:4–6). "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul," more desired than gold and sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:7–11). David asks God to cleanse him and prays, "Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight" (Psalm 19:12–14).
Psalms 19.whereWeAre: Psalm 18 praised God the rescuer. Psalm 19 praises God whose glory the heavens declare and whose law is perfect. Psalms 20 and 21 are prayers for the king in battle.

Psalms 20.summary: The people pray that the LORD will hear the king in the day of trouble and send him help from the sanctuary (Psalm 20:1–4). They will rejoice in his salvation, for "the LORD saveth his anointed" (Psalm 20:5–6). "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7–9).
Psalms 20.whereWeAre: Psalm 19 ended with a prayer for acceptable words. Psalm 20 is the people's prayer for their king before battle: "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD" (Psalm 20:7). Psalm 21 gives thanks for his victory.

Psalms 21.summary: The king rejoices in the LORD's strength, for God has given him his heart's desire, life, and a crown of gold (Psalm 21:1–6). "For the king trusteth in the LORD," and he shall not be moved (Psalm 21:7). God's hand will find out all his enemies (Psalm 21:8–12). The psalm ends, "Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength" (Psalm 21:13).
Psalms 21.whereWeAre: Psalm 20 prayed for the king before battle. Psalm 21 thanks God for answering, giving the king life, honor, and victory. Psalm 22 turns to a cry of deep suffering.

Psalms 22.summary: David cries, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" yet remembers that his fathers trusted God and were delivered (Psalm 22:1–5). He is mocked by those who say, "He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him" (Psalm 22:6–11). Enemies surround him like bulls and dogs; "they pierced my hands and my feet" and cast lots for his clothing (Psalm 22:12–18). He asks God to save him, and then he praises God in the congregation for hearing him (Psalm 22:19–25). All the ends of the world will turn to the LORD, "For the kingdom is the LORD'S" (Psalm 22:26–31).
Psalms 22.whereWeAre: Psalm 21 celebrated the king's victory. Psalm 22 begins, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Psalm 22:1), the words Jesus cried from the cross, and ends in praise. Psalm 23 follows with the LORD as shepherd.

Psalms 23.summary: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want," David says, for God leads him to green pastures and still waters (Psalm 23:1–3). "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me" (Psalm 23:4). God prepares a table before him, and "I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever" (Psalm 23:5–6).
Psalms 23.whereWeAre: Psalm 22 moved from abandonment to praise. Psalm 23 is David's song of trust: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). Psalm 24 welcomes the King of glory.

Psalms 24.summary: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof" (Psalm 24:1–2). The one who may ascend the hill of the LORD is the one with "clean hands, and a pure heart" (Psalm 24:3–6). The gates are told to lift up their heads so the King of glory may come in: "The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory" (Psalm 24:7–10).
Psalms 24.whereWeAre: Psalm 23 ended with dwelling in the house of the LORD. Psalm 24 asks who may climb God's holy hill and calls the gates to open for the King of glory. Psalm 25 is a prayer for guidance and forgiveness.

Psalms 25.summary: David lifts up his soul to God and asks not to be ashamed (Psalm 25:1–3). "Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths," he prays, and asks God to remember not the sins of his youth (Psalm 25:4–7). The LORD guides the meek, and "The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him" (Psalm 25:8–14). David asks God to turn to him in his loneliness, forgive his sins, and redeem Israel (Psalm 25:15–22).
Psalms 25.whereWeAre: Psalm 24 welcomed the King of glory. In Psalm 25, an acrostic, David asks God to teach him his paths and forgive the sins of his youth. Psalm 26 asks God to test his heart.

Psalms 26.summary: David asks the LORD to judge him, for he has walked in integrity (Psalm 26:1–3). He has not sat with vain persons, and he washes his hands in innocency at God's altar (Psalm 26:4–7). "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house," he says (Psalm 26:8). He asks not to be gathered with sinners, and he will bless the LORD in the congregations (Psalm 26:9–12).
Psalms 26.whereWeAre: Psalm 25 asked for guidance and pardon. In Psalm 26 David asks God to examine him and says he loves the house of the LORD. Psalm 27 is a song of confidence.

Psalms 27.summary: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" (Psalm 27:1–3). David's one desire is to "dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life" (Psalm 27:4–6). He asks God not to hide his face, saying that even if his father and mother forsake him, the LORD will take him up (Psalm 27:7–12). He ends, "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage" (Psalm 27:13–14).
Psalms 27.whereWeAre: Psalm 26 spoke of loving God's house. Psalm 27 begins, "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" (Psalm 27:1), and longs to dwell in his house. Psalm 28 cries out for help.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Trusts God as his light and longs for his house.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hides David in the day of trouble.

keyThemes.explanation: With God as his light, David fears no one.
David's greatest wish is to be near God.
David tells others to wait and take courage.

Psalms 28.summary: David cries to the LORD, his rock, not to be silent (Psalm 28:1–2). He asks God not to draw him away with the wicked, and to repay them for their deeds (Psalm 28:3–5). "Blessed be the LORD, because he hath heard the voice of my supplications" (Psalm 28:6–7). The LORD is the strength of his people, and David asks God to save and feed them (Psalm 28:8–9).
Psalms 28.whereWeAre: Psalm 27 ended, "Wait on the LORD" (Psalm 27:14). In Psalm 28 David cries for help and then blesses God for hearing him. Psalm 29 praises the voice of the LORD in the storm.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Cries for help and blesses God for hearing.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The strength and shield of his people.

keyThemes.explanation: David asks God not to be silent.
David blesses God for hearing him.
David asks God to feed and carry his people.

Psalms 29.summary: David calls the mighty to give the LORD the glory due his name (Psalm 29:1–2). "The voice of the LORD" thunders over the waters, breaks the cedars, divides the flames of fire, and shakes the wilderness (Psalm 29:3–9). The LORD sits as King for ever and "will bless his people with peace" (Psalm 29:10–11).
Psalms 29.whereWeAre: Psalm 28 ended with a prayer for God's people. Psalm 29 hears "the voice of the LORD" seven times in a mighty storm and ends with peace for his people. Psalm 30 gives thanks for healing.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Calls the mighty to worship.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Whose voice thunders in the storm and who blesses his people with peace.

keyThemes.explanation: Even the mighty are called to worship the LORD.
The storm shows the power of God's voice.
The God of the storm gives his people peace.

Psalms 30.summary: David praises the LORD for lifting him up and healing him (Psalm 30:1–3). "For his anger endureth but a moment... weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Psalm 30:4–5). In his prosperity he thought he would never be moved, but when God hid his face, he cried for mercy (Psalm 30:6–10). "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing," he says (Psalm 30:11–12).
Psalms 30.whereWeAre: Psalm 29 promised the LORD's people peace. Psalm 30 thanks God for healing: "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Psalm 30:5). Psalm 31 is a prayer of trust in trouble.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Thanks God for healing him.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Turns mourning into dancing.

keyThemes.explanation: God brought David up from the grave.
God's anger is short, but his favor is for life.
God turns grief into joy.

Psalms 31.summary: David asks the LORD to be his rock and fortress and prays, "Into thine hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:1–8). He is consumed with grief, forgotten "as a dead man out of mind," and slandered by many (Psalm 31:9–13). "But I trusted in thee, O LORD," he says, "My times are in thy hand" (Psalm 31:14–18). He praises God's great goodness and tells the saints, "Be of good courage" (Psalm 31:19–24).
Psalms 31.whereWeAre: Psalm 30 turned mourning into dancing. In Psalm 31 David commits his spirit into God's hand amid enemies and grief, words Jesus prayed on the cross. Psalm 32 celebrates the joy of being forgiven.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Commits his spirit into God's hand.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: David's rock and fortress, who hides him from his enemies.

keyThemes.explanation: David trusts his life into God's hands.

keyThemes.theme: My times are in God's hand
keyThemes.explanation: David trusts God with every part of his life.
God stores up goodness for those who fear him.

explainedReferences.explanation: Jesus speaks the psalm's words commending his spirit into God's hands.

Psalms 32.summary: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered" (Psalm 32:1–2). While David kept silent, his bones grew old, but when he confessed his sin, God forgave him (Psalm 32:3–5). God is his hiding place, and God promises, "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way" (Psalm 32:6–9). Mercy surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD (Psalm 32:10–11).
Psalms 32.whereWeAre: Psalm 31 ended with courage for all who hope in the LORD. Psalm 32 tells of David's misery while he hid his sin and his joy when he confessed it. Psalm 33 calls the righteous to praise.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Confesses his sin and is forgiven.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Forgives and promises to guide.

keyThemes.explanation: Those whose sins are covered are blessed.
Hiding sin brings misery, but confessing it brings forgiveness.
God promises to teach the way to go.

explainedReferences.explanation: David's words about forgiven sin.

Psalms 33.summary: The righteous are called to praise the LORD with harp and a new song (Psalm 33:1–3). "By the word of the LORD were the heavens made," for "he spake, and it was done" (Psalm 33:4–9). "Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD," for he sees all people (Psalm 33:10–15). No king is saved by an army, but the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him (Psalm 33:16–22).
Psalms 33.whereWeAre: Psalm 32 ended, "Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, ye righteous" (Psalm 32:11). Psalm 33 picks up that call and praises God who made the heavens by his word. Psalm 34 is David's song after a narrow escape.

keyFigures.name: The righteous
keyFigures.role: Called to sing a new song.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Made the heavens by his word and watches those who fear him.

keyThemes.explanation: God's people praise him with music and joy.
God made the heavens by speaking.
Safety comes from God, not from horses or armies.

Psalms 34.summary: David blesses the LORD at all times and says, "I sought the LORD, and he heard me" (Psalm 34:1–6). "The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him" (Psalm 34:7). He invites others, "O taste and see that the LORD is good" (Psalm 34:8–10). He teaches children to keep their tongues from evil and to seek peace (Psalm 34:11–14). "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart," and he keeps all the bones of the righteous (Psalm 34:15–22).
Psalms 34.whereWeAre: Psalm 33 praised God who watches over those who fear him. In Psalm 34, after escaping from Abimelech, David invites others: "O taste and see that the LORD is good" (Psalm 34:8). Psalm 35 asks God to fight his enemies.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Praises God after escaping from Abimelech.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hears the poor and delivers the righteous.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Encamps around those who fear God.

keyThemes.explanation: David blesses the LORD in every situation.
Those who trust God find that he is good.
God is close to those with broken hearts.

explainedReferences.explanation: Instructions about speech, peace, and the righteous.

Psalms 35.summary: David asks the LORD to take up shield and spear against those who fight him (Psalm 35:1–10). False witnesses repay him evil for good, though he mourned when they were sick (Psalm 35:11–16). He asks, "Lord, how long wilt thou look on?" and asks God not to let those who hate him without cause rejoice (Psalm 35:17–26). He will speak of God's righteousness all day long (Psalm 35:27–28).
Psalms 35.whereWeAre: Psalm 34 promised that the LORD delivers the righteous. In Psalm 35 David asks God to fight against those who hate him without cause. Psalm 36 contrasts the wicked with God's lovingkindness.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Asks God to fight against his false accusers.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Delivers the poor from those too strong for them.

keyFigures.name: The false witnesses
keyFigures.role: Repay David evil for good.

keyThemes.explanation: David asks God to fight for him.
David's enemies repay his kindness with cruelty.
David promises to tell of God's righteousness.

explainedReferences.explanation: Being hated without a cause.

Psalms 36.summary: The wicked man has no fear of God, flatters himself, and plots evil on his bed (Psalm 36:1–4). "Thy mercy, O LORD, is in the heavens," and people take refuge under the shadow of God's wings (Psalm 36:5–8). "For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light" (Psalm 36:9). David asks God to continue his lovingkindness, and the workers of iniquity fall (Psalm 36:10–12).
Psalms 36.whereWeAre: Psalm 35 asked God to defend David. Psalm 36 describes the wicked man's pride, then praises God's mercy, "For with thee is the fountain of life" (Psalm 36:9). Psalm 37 teaches patience when the wicked prosper.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Contrasts the wicked with God's mercy.

keyFigures.name: The wicked man
keyFigures.role: Has no fear of God and plots evil.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The fountain of life.

keyThemes.explanation: The wicked flatter themselves and plot evil.
God's mercy reaches to the heavens.
In God's light we see light.

explainedReferences.explanation: The declaration that there is no fear of God before their eyes.

Psalms 37.summary: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers," for they will soon wither like grass (Psalm 37:1–2). "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart" (Psalm 37:3–8). The wicked will be cut off, "But the meek shall inherit the earth" (Psalm 37:9–22). The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD, and David has never seen the righteous forsaken (Psalm 37:23–31). The wicked pass away, but the salvation of the righteous is of the LORD (Psalm 37:32–40).
Psalms 37.whereWeAre: Psalm 36 ended with the workers of iniquity fallen. Psalm 37 tells the righteous, "Fret not thyself because of evildoers" (Psalm 37:1), for the meek shall inherit the earth. Psalm 38 is a prayer of a sick and sorry man.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Old now, he teaches patience with the wicked.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Orders the steps of the good man and saves the righteous.

keyThemes.explanation: The righteous need not worry when the wicked prosper.
Those who trust and delight in God receive the desires of their heart.
God gives the land to the meek, not the wicked.

Psalms 38.summary: David asks the LORD not to rebuke him in wrath, for God's arrows stick fast in him (Psalm 38:1–2). His body is sick and his iniquities are like a heavy burden over his head (Psalm 38:3–10). His friends stand far off, and his enemies plot against him (Psalm 38:11–12). He hopes in the LORD, confesses his sin, and asks, "Forsake me not, O LORD" (Psalm 38:13–22).
Psalms 38.whereWeAre: Psalm 37 promised that God upholds the righteous. In Psalm 38 David suffers in body and spirit because of his sin and asks God not to forsake him. Psalm 39 reflects on how short life is.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Suffers for his sin and asks God not to forsake him.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The God David hopes in.

keyThemes.explanation: David feels his sin like a heavy burden.
Even friends keep their distance.
David still waits for the LORD to answer.

Psalms 39.summary: David kept silent before the wicked until his heart burned within him (Psalm 39:1–3). He prays, "LORD, make me to know mine end," for his days are only a handbreadth (Psalm 39:4–6). "And now, Lord, what wait I for? my hope is in thee," he says (Psalm 39:7–11). He asks God to hear his tears and spare him before he dies (Psalm 39:12–13).
Psalms 39.whereWeAre: Psalm 38 confessed sin in pain. In Psalm 39 David asks God to show him how frail he is and how short his days are. Psalm 40 sings of being lifted out of the pit.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Reflects on the shortness of life.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: David's hope.

keyThemes.explanation: David's days are only a handbreadth long.
When life is short, David's hope is in God.
David is a sojourner, as his fathers were.

Psalms 40.summary: "I waited patiently for the LORD," David says, and God lifted him out of the pit and "put a new song in my mouth" (Psalm 40:1–5). God did not desire sacrifice, so David says, "Lo, I come... I delight to do thy will, O my God" (Psalm 40:6–8). He has told God's righteousness in the great congregation (Psalm 40:9–10). Surrounded by trouble and sin, he asks God to make haste to help him (Psalm 40:11–17).
Psalms 40.whereWeAre: Psalm 39 asked God to spare David before he dies. Psalm 40 thanks God for lifting him "out of an horrible pit" (Psalm 40:2) and putting a new song in his mouth. Psalm 41 closes Book One.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Thanks God for lifting him from the pit.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hears David's cry and sets his feet on a rock.

keyThemes.explanation: David waited for God, and God lifted him up.
God's rescue gives David a new song to sing.
God wants obedience more than sacrifice.

explainedReferences.explanation: About sacrifice and doing God's will.

Psalms 41.summary: "Blessed is he that considereth the poor," for the LORD will keep him and strengthen him when he is sick (Psalm 41:1–3). David asks for healing while his enemies whisper that he will die (Psalm 41:4–8). Even "mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted" has lifted up his heel against him (Psalm 41:9). He asks God to raise him up, and Book One ends, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen" (Psalm 41:10–13).
Psalms 41.whereWeAre: Psalm 40 ended with a cry for help. Psalm 41 blesses those who care for the poor and grieves a friend's betrayal, then closes Book One with "Amen, and Amen" (Psalm 41:13). Book Two begins with Psalm 42.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays for healing and grieves a friend's betrayal.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Keeps the one who considers the poor.

keyFigures.name: David's familiar friend
keyFigures.role: Lifts up his heel against David.

keyThemes.explanation: God blesses those who care for the poor.
Even a trusted friend turns against David.
Book One ends by blessing the LORD for ever.

explainedReferences.explanation: About a trusted companion raising his heel against him.

Psalms 42.summary: The psalmist thirsts for God "as the hart panteth after the water brooks," remembering how he once went with the crowd to the house of God (Psalm 42:1–4). Enemies ask him daily, "Where is thy God?" and he answers himself, "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? ... hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him" (Psalm 42:5–10). He ends by repeating that hope, calling God "the health of my countenance, and my God" (Psalm 42:11).
Psalms 42.whereWeAre: Book One ended with David's doxology, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen" (Psalm 41:13). Psalm 42 opens Book Two with a different voice: a worshiper cut off from the temple, panting for God "as the hart panteth after the water brooks" (Psalm 42:1), who keeps telling his own soul to hope. Psalm 43 continues the same prayer and ends with the same refrain.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Commands his lovingkindness by day and gives the psalmist a song in the night, even while he feels forgotten (Psalm 42:8–9).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyFigures.name: The enemy
keyFigures.role: Taunts the psalmist daily, asking, "Where is thy God?" (Psalm 42:3,10).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalmist compares his longing for God to a deer's thirst for water.
Remembering past worship with the crowd only deepens his sorrow now that he is cut off from it.
He repeatedly commands his own soul to hope in God even while feeling forgotten.

Psalms 43.summary: The psalmist asks God to judge his cause against "an ungodly nation" and "the deceitful and unjust man" (Psalm 43:1–2). He asks God to send out his light and truth to lead him back to God's holy hill and altar, where he will praise him with the harp (Psalm 43:3–4). He ends, "hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God" (Psalm 43:5).
Psalms 43.whereWeAre: Psalm 42 ended, "hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him" (Psalm 42:11). Psalm 43 continues that same prayer without a break, asking God to judge the psalmist's cause and bring him back to the altar, and closes with the identical refrain. Psalm 44 turns from one voice to the whole nation's lament.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to judge the psalmist's cause and send his light and truth to lead him home (Psalm 43:1,3).

keyFigures.name: The ungodly nation
keyFigures.role: The deceitful and unjust people the psalmist asks God to deliver him from (Psalm 43:1).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalmist asks God to judge his cause against deceitful opponents.
He longs to return to God's altar and praise him with music.
He repeats the command to his own soul to hope in God despite present trouble.

Psalms 44.summary: Israel recalls how God drove out the nations and planted their fathers in the land, not by their own sword, but by God's hand (Psalm 44:1–3). Yet now God has cast them off, scattered them among the heathen, and made them "a reproach to our neighbours" even though "yet have we not forgotten thee" (Psalm 44:9–17). Paul later quotes their cry, "we are counted as sheep for the slaughter" (Psalm 44:22; Romans 8:36), and the psalm ends asking God to "arise for our help" (Psalm 44:26).
Psalms 44.whereWeAre: Psalm 43 ended with one voice still hoping in God. Psalm 44 shifts to the whole nation speaking as "we," recalling how God drove out the heathen for their fathers, then asking why he now lets them be slaughtered like sheep even though they have not forgotten him (Psalm 44:17,22). Psalm 45 turns from national complaint to a royal wedding song.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Drove out the nations for Israel's fathers but now seems to have cast off his people (Psalm 44:1–3,9).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Speaks throughout as "we," recalling God's past deliverance and pleading with him over a present defeat (Psalm 44:1,17,23–26).

keyThemes.explanation: Israel recalls how God gave their fathers the land by his own power, not their own.
The nation is defeated and scorned even though it has kept covenant with God.
The psalm closes by asking God to rise and redeem his people for his mercy's sake.

explainedReferences.explanation: About being counted as sheep for slaughter.

Psalms 45.summary: The psalmist's heart overflows with "a good matter" for the king, praising him as "fairer than the children of men" and mighty in battle for truth and righteousness (Psalm 45:1–4). "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever," he says, for God has anointed the king above his fellows (Psalm 45:6–7). The bride is told to forget her own people and honor her new husband, and the psalm promises the king's name will be remembered in every generation (Psalm 45:10–17).
Psalms 45.whereWeAre: Psalm 44 ended with Israel's national complaint. Psalm 45 turns to a royal wedding, praising the king's splendor and justice and blessing the bride who joins his household; Hebrews later quotes its words about the king's throne as words about the Son (Psalm 45:6–7; Hebrews 1:8–9). Psalm 46 answers with a hymn of God as refuge in upheaval.

keyFigures.name: The king
keyFigures.role: Praised as fairer than other men, mighty in battle, and anointed by God above his fellows (Psalm 45:2,7).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyFigures.name: The daughter
keyFigures.role: The bride told to forget her own people and honor the king as her lord (Psalm 45:10–11).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalm celebrates a king's wedding with praise for his splendor and strength.
The king is praised for loving righteousness and hating wickedness.
The bride's new loyalty to the king pictures a covenant bond sealed with joy.

explainedReferences.explanation: The royal psalm addressing the king's throne and anointing.

Psalms 46.summary: God is "a very present help in trouble," so the psalmist will not fear even if the earth is removed and the mountains shake in the sea (Psalm 46:1–3). A river makes glad the city of God, who helps her "right early" while nations rage and kingdoms fall (Psalm 46:4–6). The refrain declares, "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge," and God tells the nations, "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:7–11).
Psalms 46.whereWeAre: Psalm 45 praised an earthly king's wedding. Psalm 46 praises God himself as "our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble," even if the earth gives way and the mountains fall into the sea (Psalm 46:1–2); its refrain, "The LORD of hosts is with us," inspired Martin Luther's hymn A Mighty Fortress Is Our God. Psalm 47 continues the theme of God's kingship with a shout of praise.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: A refuge and present help who makes wars cease and tells the nations, "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:1,9–10).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: God is a steady refuge even if the earth itself gives way.
God's presence in the city of Zion keeps it from being moved.
God ends wars and tells the nations to be still and know him.

Psalms 47.summary: The psalmist calls all people to clap and shout, for "the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth" (Psalm 47:1–2). "God is gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet," and the psalmist calls for singing praises to him as King (Psalm 47:5–7). He closes, "God reigneth over the heathen... the princes of the people are gathered together... for the shields of the earth belong unto God" (Psalm 47:8–9).
Psalms 47.whereWeAre: Psalm 46 called the nations to "be still, and know" that God is God (Psalm 46:10). Psalm 47 answers with a shout: "O clap your hands, all ye people... God is gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet" (Psalm 47:1,5). Psalm 48 continues by praising Zion as the city of the great King.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Praised as "a great King over all the earth" who subdues nations and reigns over the heathen (Psalm 47:2,8).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: All peoples are called to clap and shout to God.
God is praised as a great King who is gone up with a shout and trumpet.
God subdues the nations and is exalted over all the earth.

Psalms 48.summary: "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God," beautiful mount Zion, "the city of the great King" (Psalm 48:1–2). Kings who assembled against her were seized with fear and fled, for "God is known in her palaces for a refuge" (Psalm 48:3–8). The psalmist calls worshipers to walk about Zion and mark her towers and bulwarks, "that ye may tell it to the generation following" (Psalm 48:12–14).
Psalms 48.whereWeAre: Psalm 47 praised God as King over all the earth. Psalm 48 praises Zion as his city, "the joy of the whole earth," and invites worshipers to walk about it and count its towers to tell the next generation (Psalm 48:2,12–13). Psalm 49 turns from Zion's praise to a wisdom poem about wealth and death.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Known in Zion's palaces as a refuge who scatters kings who assemble against the city (Psalm 48:3-4,8).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: Mount Zion is praised as the beautiful city of the great King.
Kings who gathered against Zion fled in fear because God defends her.
Worshipers are told to walk Zion's walls and tell the next generation what they see.

Psalms 49.summary: The psalmist calls all people, "both low and high, rich and poor," to hear his wisdom and his "dark saying upon the harp" (Psalm 49:1–4). No one can "by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him," for the redemption of a soul is costly and ceases for ever (Psalm 49:7–9). "Like sheep they are laid in the grave," yet "God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave: for he shall receive me" (Psalm 49:14–15).
Psalms 49.whereWeAre: Psalm 48 praised Zion's towers for the next generation to see. Psalm 49 turns to a wisdom poem for "all ye people," rich and poor together, teaching that no one can pay God a ransom to escape death, however much wealth they gain (Psalm 49:1–2,7). Psalm 50 continues with God himself calling the earth to judgment.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Able to redeem the psalmist's soul from the grave, unlike any ransom a person could pay (Psalm 49:15).

keyFigures.name: Sons of Korah
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the singers for this psalm; a family of Levite temple musicians (1 Chronicles 6:31–37).

keyThemes.explanation: No amount of wealth can ransom a person from death.
Wise and foolish alike die and leave their wealth to others.
The psalmist trusts that God, not status or wealth, will redeem his soul.

Psalms 50.summary: "The mighty God, even the LORD, hath spoken, and called the earth" to witness his judgment of his people (Psalm 50:1–4). God says he does not need their sacrifices, for "every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills" (Psalm 50:9–12); instead he wants them to "offer unto God thanksgiving" and call on him in trouble (Psalm 50:14–15). To the wicked he says, "thou givest thy mouth to evil," warning, "consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces" (Psalm 50:16–22).
Psalms 50.whereWeAre: Psalm 49 warned that wealth cannot ransom anyone from death. Psalm 50, the first psalm titled for Asaph, pictures God himself calling the whole earth to judgment, telling his people he wants "thanksgiving" and obedience, not empty sacrifices he does not need (Psalm 50:1,14). Psalm 51 follows with David's own confession after failing to live that way.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Calls the earth to witness as he judges his people for empty ritual and the wicked for hypocrisy (Psalm 50:1,4,16).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist; one of David's chief musicians (1 Chronicles 16:5).

keyThemes.explanation: God summons heaven and earth to witness his judgment of his people.
God says he needs no sacrifices but wants genuine thanksgiving and obedience.
God rebukes the wicked for reciting his words while living dishonestly.

Psalms 51.summary: David asks God for mercy "according to thy lovingkindness," to "blot out my transgressions" and "wash me throughly from mine iniquity" (Psalm 51:1–2). He confesses, "against thee, thee only, have I sinned," and asks God to "create in me a clean heart... and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 51:4,10). He says "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit," and prays for Zion's good, promising to teach other sinners God's ways (Psalm 51:13,17–18).
Psalms 51.whereWeAre: Psalm 50 pictured God calling for honest worship, not empty ritual. Psalm 51 is David's own confession after Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba, asking God to "blot out my transgressions" and "create in me a clean heart" (Psalm 51:1,10; 2 Samuel 12). Psalm 52 answers a different betrayal, Doeg's report that led Saul to kill the priests at Nob.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked for mercy, cleansing, and a renewed heart, and praised as desiring a broken spirit over sacrifice (Psalm 51:1,10,17).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Confesses his sin after Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12) and asks for a clean heart.

keyThemes.explanation: David openly admits his sin is against God and asks to be cleansed.
He asks God to create a clean heart and a right spirit within him.
David promises to teach other sinners and prays for Zion once his joy is restored.

explainedReferences.explanation: Being justified in his sayings.

Psalms 52.summary: David asks the "mighty man" why he boasts in mischief, for "the goodness of God endureth continually" (Psalm 52:1). This man "made not God his strength; but trusted in the abundance of his riches," so "God shall likewise destroy thee for ever" and "root thee out of the land of the living" (Psalm 52:5,7). David says, "I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I trust in the mercy of God for ever and ever" (Psalm 52:8).
Psalms 52.whereWeAre: Psalm 51 was David's confession of his own sin. Psalm 52 answers someone else's: Doeg the Edomite, whose report to Saul led to the massacre of the priests at Nob, is warned that God will destroy him though he trusts in his riches (Psalm 52:1,5,7; 1 Samuel 22). Psalm 53 returns to a wider lament over human corruption.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Will destroy the man who trusts in riches instead of God, while David trusts in his mercy for ever (Psalm 52:5,8).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Warns the mighty man who trusts in riches rather than God.

keyFigures.name: The mighty man
keyFigures.role: Boasts in mischief and trusts in his riches rather than God, after the pattern of Doeg's report to Saul (Psalm 52:1,7; 1 Samuel 22:9).

keyThemes.explanation: A powerful man boasts in mischief and a deceitful tongue.
God will destroy and uproot the one who trusts in riches instead of him.
David pictures himself as a green olive tree trusting in God's mercy forever.

Psalms 53.summary: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God," and God looks down to find none who seek him, for "every one of them is gone back" (Psalm 53:1–3). The workers of iniquity "eat up my people as they eat bread" and "have not called upon God," yet they will be put to shame (Psalm 53:4–5). The psalm ends longing for Israel's salvation to come out of Zion, so that "Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad" (Psalm 53:6).
Psalms 53.whereWeAre: Psalm 52 condemned one man who trusted in his riches instead of God. Psalm 53 widens the lament to all humanity, reworking Psalm 14 with "God" in place of "the LORD": "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Psalm 53:1; Psalm 14:1). Psalm 54 follows with David's own prayer when the Ziphites betrayed his hiding place to Saul.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Looks down from heaven and finds none who seek him, then scatters those who oppress his people (Psalm 53:2–3,5).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Laments human corruption and longs for Israel's deliverance.

keyThemes.explanation: The fool denies God, and none are found who seek him.
The wicked devour God's people as if eating bread, without calling on him.
The psalm ends longing for God to bring salvation and gladness to Israel.

Psalms 54.summary: David asks God to save him "by thy name" and judge him "by thy strength," for strangers and oppressors "have not set God before them" (Psalm 54:1,3). He declares, "God is mine helper: the Lord is with them that uphold my soul," and asks that his enemies be cut off (Psalm 54:4–5). He promises to "freely sacrifice" to God, for "he hath delivered me out of all trouble" (Psalm 54:6–7).
Psalms 54.whereWeAre: Psalm 53 longed for Israel's salvation in general terms. Psalm 54 is David's own cry for rescue after the Ziphites told Saul where he was hiding, trusting that "God is mine helper" even though strangers rise against him (Psalm 54:3–4; 1 Samuel 23:19). Psalm 55 continues with a prayer against a deeper betrayal, that of a close friend.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: David's helper who upholds his soul and delivers him from his enemies (Psalm 54:4,7).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays for rescue after the Ziphites betrayed his hiding place to Saul.

keyThemes.explanation: David asks God to save him from strangers who rise against him.
He declares that God is his helper who upholds his soul.
David promises a freewill offering because God has delivered him from trouble.

Psalms 55.summary: David mourns that "fearfulness and trembling are come upon me" because of violence and strife in the city, wishing he had "wings like a dove" to fly away (Psalm 55:4–6). His pain comes not from an enemy but from "a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance," who once walked with him to God's house (Psalm 55:12–14). He urges, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee," while trusting that "bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days" (Psalm 55:22–23).
Psalms 55.whereWeAre: Psalm 54 was David's prayer against strangers who betrayed him. Psalm 55 goes deeper, grieving a close friend's betrayal: "it was thou, a man mine equal... we took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company" (Psalm 55:13–14), before urging, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee" (Psalm 55:22). Psalm 56 follows with David fleeing among the Philistines in Gath.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Will sustain the one who casts his burden on him and bring down bloody and deceitful men (Psalm 55:22–23).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Grieves betrayal by a close friend and urges trust in God.

keyFigures.name: David's familiar friend
keyFigures.role: A trusted equal and acquaintance who turns against him despite their shared worship (Psalm 55:13–14,20).

keyThemes.explanation: The deepest wound comes from a trusted friend, not a stranger.
David prays three times a day amid violence and strife in the city.
He urges casting one's burden on the LORD, who will sustain the righteous.

Psalms 56.summary: Surrounded by enemies who "would swallow me up," David says, "what time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" and "will not fear what flesh can do unto me" (Psalm 56:1–4). He is confident God keeps count of his sorrow: "put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?" (Psalm 56:8). He ends, "In God have I put my trust: I will not be afraid what man can do unto me," for God has delivered his soul from death (Psalm 56:11,13).
Psalms 56.whereWeAre: Psalm 55 ended by urging trust in God amid betrayal. Psalm 56 is David's prayer from the time the Philistines seized him in Gath, declaring, "what time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" while confident God keeps every tear "in thy book" (Psalm 56:3,8; 1 Samuel 21:10–15). Psalm 57 follows with David hiding from Saul in a cave.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The one David trusts instead of fearing man, who keeps every tear in his book and delivers his soul from death (Psalm 56:3,8,13).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Trusts God while fleeing the Philistines in Gath.

keyThemes.explanation: David is surrounded by enemies who wrest his words and watch his steps.
He repeats that he trusts God's word instead of fearing what flesh can do.
He trusts that God keeps a record of every tear he sheds.

Psalms 57.summary: David takes refuge "in the shadow of thy wings" while his soul is "among lions" whose "teeth are spears and arrows" (Psalm 57:1,4). Though his enemies dug a pit for him, they fell into it themselves, and his heart becomes "fixed": "I will sing and give praise" (Psalm 57:6–7). He resolves, "I myself will awake early," to "praise thee, O Lord, among the people" and sing among the nations (Psalm 57:8–9).
Psalms 57.whereWeAre: Psalm 56 was David's prayer while a captive among the Philistines. Psalm 57 moves to another danger, David hiding from Saul in a cave, taking refuge "in the shadow of thy wings" until his heart is "fixed" enough to sing at dawn (Psalm 57:1,7–8; 1 Samuel 22:1; 24:3). Psalm 58 turns from personal danger to corrupt rulers in general.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: A refuge under whose wings David hides, whose mercy and truth reach to the heavens (Psalm 57:1,10).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Hides from Saul in a cave and resolves to praise God at dawn.

keyThemes.explanation: David hides in the shadow of God's wings while surrounded by enemies like lions.
He resolves to wake early and sing praise among the nations.
He trusts that God's mercy and truth reach beyond the heavens.

Psalms 58.summary: David asks corrupt judges, "Do ye indeed speak righteousness?" for "in heart ye work wickedness" and they are "estranged from the womb," like a "deaf adder" that will not hear the charmer (Psalm 58:1–5). He asks God, "Break their teeth, O God," and pictures them melting away like a snail or an untimely birth (Psalm 58:6,8). He ends, "the righteous shall rejoice when he seeth the vengeance," so that people will say, "Verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth" (Psalm 58:10–11).
Psalms 58.whereWeAre: Psalm 57 was David's personal prayer in danger. Psalm 58 widens to accuse unjust rulers in general: "do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?" he asks, comparing them to a "deaf adder" that will not listen to any charmer (Psalm 58:1,4). Psalm 59 returns to David's own danger, the night Saul's men watched his house.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to break the teeth of the wicked and shown to be "a God that judgeth in the earth" (Psalm 58:6,11).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Accuses corrupt rulers and appeals to God for justice.

keyFigures.name: The wicked judges
keyFigures.role: Rulers who speak wickedness instead of righteousness and refuse correction, like a deaf adder (Psalm 58:1-2,4).

keyThemes.explanation: Rulers who should judge uprightly instead work wickedness.
David asks God to break the strength of violent men.
The psalm ends confident that God judges justly in the earth.

Psalms 59.summary: David asks God to deliver him from enemies who "lie in wait for my soul" though he has done no wrong, "not for my transgression, nor for my sin" (Psalm 59:1,3). He compares them to dogs that "make a noise... and go round about the city" every evening, belching out threats (Psalm 59:6–7). Yet he trusts, "God is my defence," and promises to "sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning," for God has been his refuge "in the day of my trouble" (Psalm 59:9,16).
Psalms 59.whereWeAre: Psalm 58 condemned corrupt rulers in general. Psalm 59 returns to David's own danger, the night Saul's men "watched the house to kill him," as he calls God his "defence" while his enemies prowl the city "like a dog" (Psalm 59:1,9; 1 Samuel 19:11). Psalm 60 follows with a national lament after military defeat.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: David's defence and refuge who will let him see his desire upon his enemies (Psalm 59:9,16).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays for deliverance the night Saul's men watched his house to kill him.

keyFigures.name: David's enemies
keyFigures.role: Lie in wait for his soul and prowl the city at night like snarling dogs (Psalm 59:3,6,14).

keyThemes.explanation: David's enemies lie in wait for him though he has not sinned against them.
David calls God his defence and high place of refuge.
He promises to sing aloud of God's mercy in the morning.

Psalms 60.summary: Israel confesses, "O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us," asking him to "turn thyself to us again" and "heal the breaches" of the shaken land (Psalm 60:1–2). God answers that Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah are his, while Moab is his "washpot" and Edom will be conquered (Psalm 60:6–8). The psalm asks, "Wilt not thou, O God... give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man," ending, "Through God we shall do valiantly" (Psalm 60:10–12).
Psalms 60.whereWeAre: Psalm 59 was David's prayer in personal danger. Psalm 60 speaks for the whole nation after a military setback during David's wars with Aram and Edom, admitting "thou hast cast us off" before trusting that "through God we shall do valiantly" (Psalm 60:1,12; 2 Samuel 8:3–14). Psalm 61 follows with David's own prayer for refuge and for the king's long life.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Said to have cast Israel off in defeat but able to give help when human aid is vain (Psalm 60:1,11–12).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays for the nation after defeat during the wars with Aram and Edom.

keyThemes.explanation: Israel admits God has cast them off and scattered them in defeat.
The psalm declares that help from man is vain compared to God's help.
The psalm asks God to turn back to his people and heal the land's breaches.

Psalms 61.summary: David cries "from the end of the earth" for God to lead him "to the rock that is higher than I," for God has been "a shelter" and "a strong tower from the enemy" (Psalm 61:2–3). He resolves, "I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings" (Psalm 61:4). He prays for the king, "Thou wilt prolong the king's life... he shall abide before God for ever," and promises to "sing praise unto thy name for ever" (Psalm 61:6–8).
Psalms 61.whereWeAre: Psalm 60 was a national prayer after defeat. Psalm 61 is David's own prayer "from the end of the earth," asking to be led "to the rock that is higher than I" and praying that the king's years be prolonged "as many generations" (Psalm 61:2,6). Psalm 62 continues with quiet trust that God alone is a rock and salvation.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: A shelter and strong tower who is asked to prolong the king's life before him for ever (Psalm 61:3,6–7).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays to be led to God as his rock and prays for the king's life.

keyFigures.name: The king
keyFigures.role: Prayed for by name as the one whose years should be prolonged before God for ever (Psalm 61:6–7).

keyThemes.explanation: David asks to be led to the rock that is higher than himself.
He prays that the king's life and reign before God would be prolonged.
He promises to keep singing praise and performing his vows daily.

Psalms 62.summary: David repeats, "Truly my soul waiteth upon God... he only is my rock and my salvation," even while enemies plot to cast him down (Psalm 62:1–4). He urges the people, "Trust in him at all times... pour out your heart before him," warning that "men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie" (Psalm 62:8–9). He ends, "Trust not in oppression... if riches increase, set not your heart upon them," for "power belongeth unto God" and "mercy" is his too (Psalm 62:10–12).
Psalms 62.whereWeAre: Psalm 61 prayed for the king's long life. Psalm 62 is David's quiet meditation that "my soul waiteth upon God" alone as "my rock and my salvation," warning that riches and human status are "altogether lighter than vanity" (Psalm 62:1,9). Psalm 63 continues with David thirsting for God in the wilderness of Judah.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: David's rock and salvation, to whom belongs both power and mercy (Psalm 62:2,11–12).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Waits quietly on God alone and warns against trusting riches.

keyThemes.explanation: David repeats that his soul waits only on God as his rock and salvation.
He warns that people of both low and high degree are weighed as vanity.
He declares that both power and mercy belong to God alone.

Psalms 63.summary: David thirsts for God "in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is," remembering how he once saw God's power and glory in the sanctuary (Psalm 63:1–2). He says, "thy lovingkindness is better than life," and recalls God "upon my bed" and "in the night watches" (Psalm 63:3,6). He trusts, "in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice," while those who seek his life "shall fall by the sword" (Psalm 63:7,9–10).
Psalms 63.whereWeAre: Psalm 62 taught quiet trust in God alone. Psalm 63 is David's prayer in the wilderness of Judah, thirsting for God "in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is" (Psalm 63:1), remembering past worship and resting under God's wings. Psalm 64 follows with a prayer against enemies who plot in secret.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The one David thirsts for in the wilderness and takes refuge in under his wings (Psalm 63:1,7).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Thirsts for God while in the wilderness of Judah.

keyThemes.explanation: David compares his longing for God to thirst in a dry land.
He remembers seeing God's power and glory in the sanctuary.
He rejoices in the shadow of God's wings even while enemies seek his life.

Psalms 64.summary: David asks God to "hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked," whose tongues are like swords shooting "bitter words" at the innocent (Psalm 64:2–4). They search out ways to harm him, thinking "Who shall see them?" but God will suddenly wound them (Psalm 64:5,7). "So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves," and "the righteous shall be glad in the LORD, and shall trust in him" (Psalm 64:8,10).
Psalms 64.whereWeAre: Psalm 63 was David's prayer of longing in the wilderness. Psalm 64 asks God to hide him from enemies who "whet their tongue like a sword" and "shoot in secret at the perfect," trusting that God will turn their own words against them (Psalm 64:3–4,8). Psalm 65 follows with a thanksgiving for harvest and answered prayer.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Shoots down the wicked suddenly with his own arrow, turning their secret plots back on them (Psalm 64:7-8).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays for protection from secret plots and malicious words.

keyFigures.name: The wicked
keyFigures.role: Plot secretly and shoot bitter words at the innocent, thinking no one sees them (Psalm 64:2-5).

keyThemes.explanation: David's enemies plot secretly, confident no one will see their plans.
Their own words and plots turn back and fall upon them.
The righteous rejoice and trust in God once he exposes the wicked.

Psalms 65.summary: "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion," for he hears prayer and purges transgressions, and all flesh shall come to him (Psalm 65:1–3). He is "the confidence of all the ends of the earth," who stills the sea and quiets the nations by his strength (Psalm 65:5,7). He waters the earth until "the pastures are clothed with flocks... they shout for joy, they also sing" (Psalm 65:9,13).
Psalms 65.whereWeAre: Psalm 64 ended with the righteous trusting God to expose evil. Psalm 65 gives thanks for answered prayer and a rich harvest, praising God who "visitest the earth, and waterest it" until "the valleys also are covered over with corn" (Psalm 65:9,13). Psalm 66 widens the thanksgiving to call the whole earth to praise.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Hears prayer, forgives transgressions, stills the seas, and sends rain that crowns the year with abundance (Psalm 65:2-3,7,11).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Praises God for hearing prayer and sending a rich harvest.

keyThemes.explanation: God forgives sins and draws all flesh to approach him.
God stills the roaring seas and the tumult of the peoples.
God waters the land so that it overflows with grain and flocks.

Psalms 66.summary: "Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands," for he is terrible in his works and "turned the sea into dry land" at the exodus (Psalm 66:1,3,6). "Thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried," bringing them through fire and water into a wealthy place (Psalm 66:10,12). The psalmist comes with burnt offerings to pay his vows, testifying, "verily God hath heard me; he hath attended to the voice of my prayer" (Psalm 66:13,19).
Psalms 66.whereWeAre: Psalm 65 thanked God for a harvest. Psalm 66 widens that thanksgiving, calling "all ye lands" to praise the God who "turned the sea into dry land" and tried his people as silver is tried, before the psalmist personally testifies, "God hath heard me" (Psalm 66:1,6,10,16). Psalm 67 continues the call for all nations to praise God.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Turned the sea into dry land at the exodus, tested his people like silver, and heard the psalmist's prayer (Psalm 66:6,10,19).

keyThemes.explanation: All the earth is called to make a joyful noise to God.
God tried his people like silver through fire and water.
The psalmist pays his vows and testifies that God heard his prayer.

Psalms 67.summary: The psalm echoes the priestly blessing, "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us" (Psalm 67:1). This is so "thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations," and the psalmist calls all peoples to praise God (Psalm 67:2–3). It ends, "the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us," so that "all the ends of the earth shall fear him" (Psalm 67:6–7).
Psalms 67.whereWeAre: Psalm 66 was one person's testimony that God heard his prayer. Psalm 67 is a brief blessing echoing the priestly blessing, asking God to "cause his face to shine upon us" so that his way may be known and all nations may praise him (Psalm 67:1–2; Numbers 6:24–26). Psalm 68 follows with a long hymn of God's march from Sinai to his sanctuary.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to bless his people and make his way known among all nations, who in turn will fear him (Psalm 67:1-2,7).

keyThemes.explanation: God's blessing on his people is meant to make his way known to all nations.
The psalm asks God to judge and govern the nations righteously.
All peoples and the whole earth are called to praise and fear God.

Psalms 68.summary: "Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered," for he is "a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows" who sets the solitary in families (Psalm 68:1,5–6). When God marched through the wilderness, "the earth shook... Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God," and he gave rain to his weary inheritance (Psalm 68:7–9). The psalm pictures a procession into the sanctuary with singers and musicians, declaring, "thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive," words Paul later applies to Christ's gifts to the church (Psalm 68:18,24–25; Ephesians 4:8).
Psalms 68.whereWeAre: Psalm 67 asked that all nations come to praise God. Psalm 68 answers with a long hymn of God's march from Sinai to his sanctuary, scattering his enemies and defending the fatherless and widows, with Paul later quoting its words about leading captivity captive (Psalm 68:1,5,18; Ephesians 4:8). Psalm 69 follows with a lament of shame and persecution.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Scatters his enemies, defends the fatherless and widows, and is pictured ascending on high and leading captivity captive (Psalm 68:1,5,18).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Celebrates God's march from Sinai to his sanctuary.

keyThemes.explanation: God is a father to the fatherless and a judge for widows.
The earth itself shook when God marched through the wilderness with his people.
Singers and musicians celebrate God's procession into his sanctuary.

explainedReferences.explanation: About ascending on high and gifts, with adapted wording.

Psalms 69.summary: David cries, "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul... I am come into deep waters," hated "without a cause" and bearing reproach "for thy sake" (Psalm 69:1–2,4,7). He is given "gall for my meat" and "vinegar to drink," words later connected to Jesus on the cross, and he asks God to pour out indignation on his persecutors (Psalm 69:21,24; Matthew 27:34,48). He ends praising God who "will save Zion," promising that those who love his name will dwell there (Psalm 69:35–36).
Psalms 69.whereWeAre: Psalm 68 celebrated God's victorious procession. Psalm 69 turns to deep distress, David crying, "I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing," bearing reproach "for thy sake" (Psalm 69:2,7) — words the New Testament quotes more than almost any other psalm, including Jesus's disciples recalling "the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (Psalm 69:9; John 2:17). Psalm 70 follows with a brief, urgent cry for help.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to save David from deep waters and to save Zion, where those who love his name will dwell (Psalm 69:1,35–36).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Cries out from deep distress and reproach, in words the New Testament later applies to Jesus.

keyThemes.explanation: David bears shame and reproach for God's sake, hated without cause.
He cries out from deep waters that threaten to overwhelm him.
The psalm ends trusting that God will save Zion for those who love his name.

explainedReferences.explanation: The disciples recall the psalm's words about zeal for God's house.
About reproaches falling on the speaker.
Words about a table becoming a snare and eyes growing dark.
Call for a dwelling place to become desolate.

Psalms 70.summary: David cries, "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD" (Psalm 70:1). He asks that those who seek his life be "ashamed and confounded," while those who seek God "rejoice and be glad" and say, "Let God be magnified" (Psalm 70:2,4). He ends, "I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying" (Psalm 70:5).
Psalms 70.whereWeAre: Psalm 69 was a long lament from deep distress. Psalm 70 is a short, urgent prayer reusing the ending of Psalm 40, crying "make haste, O God, to deliver me" (Psalm 70:1; Psalm 40:13–17). Psalm 71 follows with the prayer of someone now old, asking not to be abandoned in age.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to hurry to help and deliver David, who calls him "my help and my deliverer" (Psalm 70:1,5).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Prays an urgent, short cry for help, reusing Psalm 40's ending.

keyThemes.explanation: David repeats his plea for God to make haste and not delay.
He asks that those seeking his hurt be put to shame.
Those who seek God are blessed with rejoicing and gladness.

Psalms 71.summary: The psalmist, trusting God "from the womb," now asks, "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth" (Psalm 71:6,9). Enemies say "God hath forsaken him," but he resolves, "I will hope continually, and will yet praise thee more and more" (Psalm 71:11,14). "Now also when I am old and grayheaded," he prays, "forsake me not, until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come" (Psalm 71:18).
Psalms 71.whereWeAre: Psalm 70 was a short, urgent cry for help. Psalm 71 has no title, letting any older believer pray it as their own: "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth," while promising to keep telling the next generation of God's deeds (Psalm 71:9,18). Psalm 72 closes Book Two with a prayer for the king's righteous reign.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Has held up the psalmist from the womb and is asked not to forsake him in old age (Psalm 71:6,9,18).

keyThemes.explanation: The psalmist, who has trusted God from youth, prays not to be cast off in old age.
Enemies who say God has forsaken him are met with his resolve to keep hoping.
He asks for strength to keep showing God's power to the generation to come.

Psalms 72.summary: The prayer asks God to "give the king thy judgments," so he may "judge the poor of the people" and "break in pieces the oppressor" (Psalm 72:1,4). It pictures his reign bringing peace "so long as the moon endureth," with kings of Tarshish and Sheba bringing gifts and "all nations" serving him (Psalm 72:7,10–11). It closes, "blessed be the LORD God... let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen," followed by the note, "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended" (Psalm 72:18–20).
Psalms 72.whereWeAre: Psalm 71 was an aging believer's prayer. Psalm 72, titled "for Solomon," closes Book Two with a prayer for the king's righteous reign over the poor and needy, and its closing note, "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended," marks the end of this collection (Psalm 72:2,20). Book Three opens with Psalm 73's confession, "Truly God is good to Israel."

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Asked to give the king his own judgments and righteousness, so that the whole earth may be filled with his glory (Psalm 72:1,19).

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: The king prayed for in the title and the psalm itself, that he would judge the poor with righteousness and reign in peace (Psalm 72:1–4).

keyThemes.explanation: The king is prayed for as one who judges the poor and needy with righteousness.
His reign is pictured bringing abundant peace as long as the moon endures.
Distant kings bring gifts and all nations are blessed through his reign.

Psalms 73.summary: Asaph confesses, "Truly God is good to Israel," even though he nearly envied the wicked, whose "eyes stand out with fatness" while they mock, "How doth God know?" (Psalm 73:1,3,7,11). Only when he "went into the sanctuary of God" did he understand their end, set in "slippery places" and swept away "as in a moment" (Psalm 73:17-19). He concludes, "God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever," and "it is good for me to draw near to God" (Psalm 73:26,28).
Psalms 73.whereWeAre: Psalm 72 closed Book Two with David's prayers "ended" (Psalm 72:20). Psalm 73 opens Book Three with Asaph's confession that God is good to Israel, even though he nearly envied the wicked's prosperity until he went into God's sanctuary (Psalm 73:1,17). Psalm 74 turns from this personal struggle to a communal lament over the ruined sanctuary itself.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is the psalmist's portion and strength even though the wicked seem to prosper without him (Psalm 73:1,26).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Nearly envies the wicked until he understands their end in God's sanctuary.

keyFigures.name: The wicked
keyFigures.role: Prosper without trouble, speak proudly against heaven, and ask, "How doth God know?" (Psalm 73:3,8-9,11).

keyThemes.explanation: Asaph nearly stumbles seeing the wicked prosper without trouble or punishment.
Only in God's sanctuary does he come to understand the wicked's true end.
He concludes that God, not wealth or ease, is his strength and portion forever.

Psalms 74.summary: Asaph asks, "O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever?" for enemies have "cast fire into thy sanctuary" and "break down the carved work thereof" (Psalm 74:1,6-7). He recalls that God "didst divide the sea" and broke the heads of leviathan, the same God who made "the day" and "the night," "summer and winter" (Psalm 74:13-14,16-17). He asks God to "have respect unto the covenant" and "arise" to plead his own cause (Psalm 74:20,22).
Psalms 74.whereWeAre: Psalm 73 found personal perspective in God's sanctuary. Psalm 74 mourns that same sanctuary in ruins, enemies having "cast fire into thy sanctuary" (Psalm 74:7), while recalling that the same God who divided the sea also "prepared the light and the sun" (Psalm 74:13,16). Psalm 75 answers that God judges in his own chosen time.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Divided the sea and broke leviathan's heads, yet is asked why he has let his own sanctuary be destroyed (Psalm 74:1,13-14).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Laments the destroyed sanctuary and recalls God's covenant and creative power.

keyFigures.name: The enemy
keyFigures.role: Burns God's sanctuary, breaks its carved work with axes, and reproaches God's name (Psalm 74:3-7,10).

keyThemes.explanation: Enemies destroy God's dwelling place with fire and axes.
Asaph recalls God's power over the sea, day, night, and seasons as a reason to hope.
He asks God to remember his covenant and rise to defend his own name.

Psalms 75.summary: The psalmist gives thanks, for God says, "When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly" (Psalm 75:1-2). He warns the proud, "Lift not up your horn on high," for promotion comes from God alone, who "putteth down one, and setteth up another" (Psalm 75:4-7). "In the hand of the LORD there is a cup" of judgment for the wicked, while "the horns of the righteous shall be exalted" (Psalm 75:8,10).
Psalms 75.whereWeAre: Psalm 74 asked God to "arise" and defend his cause. Psalm 75 answers that God judges "when I shall receive the congregation," at the time he chooses, pouring out his cup of wrath on the wicked while lifting up the righteous (Psalm 75:2,8,10). Psalm 76 celebrates a specific victory God has already won.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Judges uprightly at his own chosen time, humbling the proud and exalting the righteous (Psalm 75:2,7,10).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
keyFigures.role: Named in the title as the psalmist. Warns the proud that only God grants promotion.

keyThemes.explanation: God judges at his own appointed time, not man's.
The psalm warns the proud not to lift up their horn against God.
The psalmist gives thanks now and promises to keep singing praises to God.

Psalms 76.summary: In Judah God is known, and "in Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion" (Psalm 76:1-2). There he broke "the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword," and at his rebuke "the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep" (Psalm 76:3,6). The psalm calls all to fear him, for he "shall cut off the spirit of princes" and is "terrible to the kings of the earth" (Psalm 76:12).
Psalms 76.whereWeAre: Psalm 75 declared that God judges in his own time. Psalm 76 celebrates a victory already won: "in Salem also is his tabernacle," where he broke "the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword" (Psalm 76:2-3). Psalm 77 turns from this celebrated victory to a psalmist's own present trouble.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Known in Zion, where he breaks the weapons of war and is terrible to the kings of the earth (Psalm 76:1-3,12).

keyFigures.name: Asaph
